mcqs.question: Why doesn't encryption alone fully prevent a man-in-the-middle attack?
options: Encryption is always breakable given enough time
Encryption slows down MITM attacks but cannot be defeated by them at all
MITM attacks only work over unencrypted UDP traffic
Without authentication, an attacker can present their own key/certificate, so the victim ends up securely talking to the attacker instead of the real party
mcqs.explanation: The missing piece is authentication — verifying identity, not just scrambling bytes. Without it, an attacker can insert their own key and the connection is 'securely' encrypted to the wrong party. MITM isn't UDP-specific, and encryption without auth doesn't fully block MITM at all, it just changes the mechanism.

mcqs.question: Why is blocking a single source IP an ineffective defense against a DDoS attack, while it might work against a basic DoS attack?
options: A DDoS attack arrives from many distributed sources simultaneously, so blocking one IP barely reduces the overall traffic
DDoS attacks always use encrypted traffic, making IPs invisible
DoS attacks cannot be blocked by IP under any circumstance
DDoS traffic never has a source IP address at all
mcqs.explanation: The 'distributed' in DDoS is exactly the defensive challenge — thousands of sources means blocking any one has negligible impact, unlike a single-source DoS where IP blocking can be effective. Encryption and IP visibility aren't the relevant factors here.

mcqs.question: A company suffers a volumetric DDoS attack despite having a well-configured firewall. Why didn't the firewall stop it?
options: The firewall's rules were misconfigured and any correct configuration would have blocked it
A volumetric attack can saturate network capacity or overwhelm the firewall's processing before traffic even reaches rule evaluation, regardless of the rules themselves
Firewalls only protect against SQL injection, not network-layer attacks
DDoS attacks bypass firewalls only when using IPv6
mcqs.explanation: Firewalls filter based on rules applied to traffic that reaches them — but sheer volume can saturate the link or the device itself before rule-based filtering ever comes into play, which is exactly why volumetric attacks need capacity-based defenses instead. This isn't a misconfiguration issue, a SQL-injection-specific concern, or an IPv6-only phenomenon.
